title: Critical Thinking · Episode 4
chapters: The lady tasting tea: how to design a fair test
Science or pseudoscience? How to tell the difference

units.t: Critical Thinking. Episode four.
In this episode: The lady tasting tea: how to design a fair test, How to judge a claim and Science or pseudoscience? How to tell the difference.
Part one. The lady tasting tea: how to design a fair test.
A scientist claimed she could taste whether the milk or the tea went into the cup first.
Working out how to test her claim properly helped shape the modern experiment.
Tea at Rothamsted.
In the early 1920s, at the Rothamsted agricultural research station north of London, the statistician Ronald Fisher offered a colleague a cup of tea.
Doctor Muriel Bristol, a scientist who studied algae, declined because he had poured the milk in after the tea.
She preferred milk first, and insisted she could taste the difference.
Fisher was sceptical.
According to later accounts from people who were there, a test was quickly arranged, and she reportedly identified the cups correctly.
Fisher used the story to open a chapter of his 1935 book The Design of Experiments.
Behind a light-hearted example lay a serious question: how do you fairly test a claim?
What would luck look like.
Fisher's key move was to assume the claim is false.
Suppose Bristol has no ability and is simply guessing.
This assumption is now called the null hypothesis.
Then ask whether her actual performance would be surprising by comparison.
His design used eight cups, four milk-first and four tea-first, in random order.
She would pick out the four milk-first cups.
There are 70 ways to choose four cups from eight, and only one is fully correct.
A guesser has a 1 in 70 chance of a perfect score, about 1.
4 per cent.
Three right and one wrong can happen 16 ways, so scoring at least three out of four by luck is 17 in 70, about 24 per cent.
That's too common to prove anything.
Decide what counts as convincing before you run the test.
Why randomise.
Why serve the cups in random order?
Imagine the four milk-first cups were all prepared and served first.
They might be slightly cooler, or the taster might notice a pattern.
Any success could then come from those clues rather than from tasting the milk.
Fisher argued that randomisation is the most reliable protection against hidden factors like these, including ones nobody has thought of.
He also stressed keeping everything else the same: the same cups, the same tea and the same amount of milk.
He developed these ideas through crop experiments at Rothamsted, where treatments were assigned to plots of land at random so that differences in soil couldn't bias the results.
Size matters.
Fisher's framework also shows why the number of trials matters.
With six cups, three of each, there are only 20 ways to choose, so even a perfect score has a 1 in 20 chance of happening by luck, or five per cent.
With just four cups, two of each, a guesser gets a perfect score one time in six.
A test that small could never convince anyone, however good the taster.
Fisher suggested treating results that would happen by chance less than about one time in 20 as worth taking seriously.
That convention later hardened into the famous 0.
05 threshold for statistical significance.
He saw it as a rough guide to which results deserve attention, not a magic line between truth and falsehood.
Trials, and a warning.
Fisher's ideas now run through modern research.
Drug trials assign patients to treatment or placebo at random and ask how likely the results would be if the drug did nothing.
Farmers test crop varieties in randomised plots.
Technology companies run A/B tests, randomly showing different web page versions to different users.
Three questions travel well.
What would I expect to see if this claim were false?
Could something else explain the result?
Was the test big enough to tell?
Yet Fisher himself erred.
In the late 1950s he argued that the smoking and lung cancer link might not be causal, suggesting an inherited factor could explain both.
Asking about hidden causes is legitimate, but the evidence against smoking became overwhelming.
Fisher was a keen pipe smoker and had consulted for the tobacco industry.
The key idea: A casual claim at afternoon tea led Ronald Fisher to ask how to test any claim fairly.
Part two. How to judge a claim.
'Scientists say…', 'A study found…'.
A practical checklist for deciding what to believe.
Not all evidence is equal.
Anecdotes, expert opinions, single studies and large reviews all count as 'evidence', but they're not equally reliable.
Personal stories and opinions sit near the bottom.
Above them come observational studies, then randomised controlled trials.
Near the top are systematic reviews and meta-analyses, which combine many good studies.
One study rarely settles a question.
Small studies can also produce dramatic results by chance.
Getting 7 heads in 10 coin flips isn't unusual; 7,000 heads in 10,000 flips would be astonishing.
A treatment that 'worked for 8 of 10 people' is far less convincing than one tested on thousands.
Surprising small-study findings often shrink in larger studies, the decline effect.
Compared with what.
Without a comparison group, you can't tell whether an improvement came from the treatment, the placebo effect or people simply getting better on their own.
The choice of comparison matters too.
A new drug that beats a sugar pill may still be worse than the treatment doctors already use, so the most useful trials test new options against standard care.
Be wary of comparisons with patients from years earlier, or with people who chose not to take part, since they may differ in many ways.
When you read about a study, ask: compared with what?
Risk needs numbers.
'Doubles your risk' sounds alarming, but if risk goes from 1 in 100,000 to 2 in 100,000, the absolute change is tiny.
Headlines prefer relative numbers because they sound bigger.
'Cuts risk by 50 per cent' might mean 2 in 1,000 falling to 1 in 1,000.
Always ask: out of how many people?
Rarity also matters.
Imagine a disease affecting 1 in 1,000 people and a test that's 99 per cent accurate.
Test 1,000 people: about 1 has the disease and tests positive, but about 10 of the 999 healthy people also test positive by mistake.
A positive result means only about a 1 in 11 chance of having it.
That's why doctors often confirm with a second test.
Who says so.
Ask who's making the claim and what they gain if you believe it.
Research funded by companies with a stake isn't automatically wrong, but it's more likely to favour the sponsor, so independent confirmation matters.
Be wary of claims that appear only on sites selling a product.
Is the source a peer-reviewed journal, a reputable organisation like the CSIRO or a university, or a press release, blog or social post?
Astronomer Carl Sagan popularised the principle that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence.
Be alert to miracle breakthroughs, 'what they don't want you to know', testimonials instead of data, attacks on mainstream experts and pressure to buy now.
Real breakthroughs are usually cautious and replicated by independent teams.
A quick checklist.
Next time you meet a claim, run through six questions.
What's the source, and could they be biased?
What kind of evidence is it: anecdote, observational study or trial?
How many people were studied?
Compared with what?
What are the absolute numbers?
And what do most experts in the field think?
You won't always have time to check everything, but even asking two or three of these questions will make you far harder to fool.
The key idea: Evidence has a hierarchy, and small studies can produce dramatic results by chance, so the weight of evidence matters more than any single study.
Part three. Science or pseudoscience? How to tell the difference.
Astrology, crystal healing and a revolutionary new diet can all sound scientific.
A few sharp questions reveal which ideas are willing to be proven wrong.
Popper and falsifiability.
In Vienna after the First World War, young Karl Popper was surrounded by bold ideas.
Einstein's relativity made a risky prediction: starlight passing the Sun should bend by a specific amount.
In 1919, expeditions led by Arthur Eddington measured starlight during a solar eclipse and supported Einstein.
The theory could have failed, and it didn't.
Some popular theories of psychology and history, by contrast, explained every possible outcome.
Popper saw that as a weakness.
His answer to the problem of separating science from non-science was falsifiability.
'All swans are white' is falsifiable: one black swan breaks it, and Europeans found black swans in Western Australia.
'Invisible fairies tend my garden but leave no trace' isn't.
Falsifiable doesn't mean false, just testable.
Ask what would prove an idea wrong.
The warning signs.
Pseudoscience is dressed up to look scientific without behaving like science.
It shows familiar warning signs.
Claims are vague, so they can't easily be checked.
Evidence comes mainly from testimonials and anecdotes rather than controlled studies.
Scientific words such as 'quantum', 'energy' and 'frequency' are borrowed for glamour without precise meaning.
When a test fails, excuses appear: the sceptic's negative energy interfered.
The idea hasn't changed for decades despite new evidence.
Critics are dismissed as closed-minded.
And there is often something to buy.
No single sign proves an idea is bogus, but when several appear together, look much more carefully before you believe or spend.
Astrology under test.
Astrology makes claims that can, in principle, be tested: your birth chart is said to reveal your personality.
In a 1985 study in the journal Nature, physicist Shawn Carlson ran a double-blind test with astrologers who had agreed to the method in advance.
They were given birth charts and asked to match each to the correct personality profile from a small set of options.
Their success rate was about what guessing would produce.
Other studies have looked for links between star signs and personality or career and generally found nothing meaningful.
Astrology can still be enjoyable, a prompt for reflection or a bit of fun.
But as a scientific claim about how people work, it hasn't passed the test.
Homeopathy in Australia.
Homeopathy was developed in Germany around 1800 by Samuel Hahnemann.
Its central idea is that a substance causing symptoms can cure similar symptoms when heavily diluted, and that more dilution makes it stronger.
Many remedies are diluted so far that, statistically, not one molecule of the original substance is likely to remain.
In 2015, Australia's National Health and Medical Research Council published a major review of the evidence.
It concluded there were no health conditions for which there was reliable evidence that homeopathy was effective.
The council warned that choosing it over proven treatments may put health at risk.
This is general information rather than medical advice.
Talk to a doctor, and healthdirect is a reliable starting point for health questions in Australia.
Self-correction, not Galileo.
Science gets things wrong all the time.
What makes it different is that it has ways of finding and fixing errors.
Studies are checked by experts, results are repeated by independent teams, and failed ideas are revised or dropped.
For decades, doctors thought stomach ulcers were mainly caused by stress.
Perth researchers Barry Marshall and Robin Warren showed that a bacterium, Helicobacter pylori, played a central role.
Marshall even swallowed a culture to prove the point.
Doctors were sceptical, but evidence won, and the pair received the 2005 Nobel Prize.
Fringe promoters often say 'they laughed at Galileo'.
But for every rejected idea later proven right, vast numbers were rejected because they were wrong.
Galileo was vindicated by his observations, not by being mocked.
Being an outsider is fine.
Avoiding tests isn't.
The key idea: A claim is scientific if some observation could show it to be false, so a theory that fits every possible result tells you nothing.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What question did the tea story lead Fisher to explore?
Answer. How to fairly test whether a claim is true.
Question two. Which kind of evidence is generally the most reliable?
Answer. A systematic review of many studies.
Question three. What makes a claim scientific, according to falsifiability?
Answer. A test could show it to be false.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
